why: It gives the one dimension of a hand-built dividing bund read from excavated ground - half a meter or less, with no core, rebuilt each season - a floor for the ridge between two plots. That small bund split one block inside a large bund to spread water evenly over it; the article does not say it separated one holder's land from another's, and the bunds between parcels in later, larger fields (the jōri grid, the Edo village) were permanent and could be wider (this project's reading; the article says only that these plots came before the handen and jōri fields), so it bounds the ridge from below and is not the width of a boundary between holdings. It describes paddies of the Yayoi and Kofun periods, roughly fifteen hundred to twenty-five hundred years ago and most of them Kofun, not of the setting's period, and the article gives the whole sentence - the width, the missing core, the rebuilding each season - as "thought to have been".

It is the plainest statement read of which settlement form was usual in Japan, and of how it differed between the west and the east. "general" and "common" are its words, with no figure and no period.
unsettled: Gives no period; a modern geographers' account of a traditional settlement form.

why: It shows the dispersed village in Japan as a set of named regions rather than a general form, which is what lets the record call it regional. Its list of irregular dispersed villages (the Tonami plain, the lower Ōi, the Sanuki and Izumo plains) ends "and others", so it shows where the form is typical, not that it is confined to those places. It names them as a modern geographer sees them and does not date each dispersal; the Heibonsha extract on the same page dates Tonami's to medieval reclamation. It gives no count. Its planned kind (the Meiji-era tondenhei villages of Hokkaido, the American township) is not premodern and is not used here.
unsettled: Names regions as a modern geographer sees them and does not date the dispersal.

why: It gives a domain seat whose lord and offices sat in the second bailey, the arrangement this page uses for where a domain's council met. The article does not say the domain's business was transacted in the second bailey, only that the lord's residence and the armaments office stood there; a 170,000-koku domain is a large one, and the arrangement is the one a fire ended in 1846.

It names the block village as the most general of the gathered forms, which puts it first among the clustered forms; it names the others without ranking them. The claim belongs to settlement geography in general, not to Japan alone (the same sentence names German and Polish round villages), and the entry gives no count or period.
unsettled: A claim of settlement geography in general with no period stated.

why: It says a tutelary shrine is found in every village and that the idea of the village as the unit of shrine and parish spread over almost the whole country under the Edo order, which is the baseline for asking whether a hamlet below the village had one. Its "every village" describes the present day, and Sonoda says the Meiji government made the village shrine as ujigami official policy, so today's uniformity is partly a Meiji product; for the Edo period it claims only that the idea spread, not that every village had a shrine. It speaks of the village, not of hamlets within it; the gods it names below the village belong to a kin group (the maki or ikke ujigami) or a single house, not to a hamlet.

It shows, in one place, both forms below the village: sections with a shrine of their own and communities with none. Its counts cover only registered shrines, and its explanations are the priest's and a shrine elder's guess. Its fourteen shrines are listed in the shrine's 1879 register and most were rebuilt in the Edo period, so the section shrines reach back at least to the late-Edo village, though the newspaper reads that register at second hand. The communities with no shrine, though, are counted today, after the 1906 merger order, so they may be what the mergers left rather than what an Edo-period village held. It is one case, which the article calls exceptional, and it gives no share.

It states in one place how the farm household shrank over the Edo period and why - the early large households of a powerful farmer with his dependents and kin breaking up into small stem-family farms - and gives one region's figures for it. It is a secondary summary for legislators, not the research itself: its Suwa figures come from Hayami Akira's book, it gives only round numbers ("about eight", "about four"), and its "stem family of about four" is a one-line summing-up.

unsettled: Registers of 1860-1875 straddle the 1868 cut-off between premodern and modern preindustrial.

why: It is where the record finds that one farm family could live under two roofs, that the second roof mostly stood within the family's own yard, and in which parts of Japan the custom was strong or thin. These are encyclopedia summaries of folklore and family-sociology fieldwork, much of it of the twentieth century - three entries note the custom is still practiced, and one that building retirement houses had lately become a fashion in part of Shiga, and the page's Edo-period material is on warrior and townsman retirement, not the village custom - so they describe a custom rather than date it within the Edo period; they give its geography only as tendencies ("strongly", "common") and give no share of households that kept a retirement house. They say only that the retirement house stood mostly within the yard, with its own entrance, and was smaller than the main house. They do not say where in the yard it stood or give its size, and they note that in fishing and mountain villages the old couple often borrowed an empty house or part of another household's instead.

It shows that in the early Edo period a plot could hold several families under several roofs while the register of houses, people and horses (the book the labor levy was drawn from) counted it as one hearth - the one case found where a register's household and a map's houses would not match one to one. It is an excerpt of an excerpt, placed by its own entry in the early part of the period, before the dependents split off into households of their own; it says nothing of how many plots were like this, nor of how the population registers of religious inquiry counted the same families, since the one-hearth count it gives is the labor-levy register's; and the same passage is on the fuller kotobank page for the house plot.

It states plainly that the carpenter and the plasterer worked away from home while the cabinetmaker worked in his own workshop, from which we take it that a carpenter needs no workshop of his own on a town map. That conclusion is ours, not the page's: the same page puts the independent master carpenter (棟梁) in a street-front house (表店), so the trade still has a frontage on the street even though its work is done on site. It is an unsigned popular history of Edo by a trade body, published in its magazine in 2003; it is written about Edo, but the split between work out on site (出職) and work at home (居職) was a general classification of the period's crafts, not only Edo's.

It says the early-modern cooper both made and sold in his own house, that coopers gathered in cooper streets in castle towns, and that some went round towns and villages mending hoops. It gives no workshop size.
It says the tatami maker worked mostly at home and sometimes out on the job, which is why the trade fits an ordinary house-shop. It says nothing of the workshop's size or where in a town it stood.

It dates the tofu maker's shop, says it spread from the towns to nearby villages, and says it sold both over the counter and from peddlers' tubs, which is why the trade draws as an ordinary shop. It cites no sources, so its dates are the encyclopedist's own. It does not date the peddling from tubs, and says shop sale and peddling are "the same today", so peddling in the period is inferred rather than shown. The trumpet-blowing peddler it mentions is from the late nineteenth century and outside the setting. It gives no premises or water supply.

It defines the apothecary as a house that made up and sold its medicines itself, the kind of trade the generic shop glyph stands for. Two modern Japanese dictionary entries for a word first recorded about 1678 and still in use in the nineteenth century. They describe Edo-period Japan and say nothing of China. "A house that compounds crude drugs and deals in Chinese medicine" is the dictionary's stock wording for a trade. The same word also names the wholesale drug merchant (yakushushō): its nineteenth-century example is Osaka's Doshomachi wholesalers. So it does not show that compounding, selling and living shared one building, and it gives no premises.

It is used for one line: that drug shops stood eave to eave in Nihonbashi Honcho from the Edo period, an example of a trade street in the great city. Its history is a single uncited line in a list of related pages (a gloss on the article on Nihonbashi Honcho, which also cites nothing and names the trade there as wholesale druggists); it gives no count of shops, no date within the Edo period, and says nothing of a small town.

It says the shogunate first confined brewing to castle towns, post towns and ports, licensed every brewer, and only in the eighteenth century let landlords brew in the villages, and that brewers commonly lent money and took pledges - which is why a county town keeps a brewer and a village does not. Signed reference entries on Japan, written by the historians (Wakita, Yunoki) whose own books they cite. The confinement to towns was a Tokugawa rice-price policy of the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, not a general premodern rule. The same entries say medieval brewers gathered in towns because brewing needed capital, not because the law required it; that from the 1730s landlord brewing spread widely through the villages; and that by the eighteenth century villages had their own sake retailers and drinking shops. Nothing here speaks to China. The only counts are for the capital, Kyoto (342 sake houses in the 1425-26 register, a brewer holding 20 to 120 jars of 2-3 koku), which are a capital's figures, not a county town's; there are no building sizes.

It says the clay hulling mill broke many grains and that the farm household ate the broken rice because it could not be shipped, which puts the hulling on the farm, before the rice left it. Its history is a paragraph, and it does not say in so many words who hulled. The broken-rice passage is cited to one town's history (Kamiichi, Toyama, 1970) and gives no date. It describes the clay-mill era that ended in the 1930s, most likely late Meiji to early Showa with its shipping of rice, not the Edo period, so it stands in for the Edo practice rather than showing it.

It attests two forms of polishing in the Edo period, the treadle mortar worked by foot and the water-driven pestle at waterwheels on a stream (several stood on Edo's Onden river, around today's Jingumae), which is why a town's polishing has two forms. Its history rests on one footnoted source, an introductory article in the Journal of the Japan Society for Precision Engineering, and the water-driven mill appears only in an uncited caption to Hokusai's print rather than in the body text. The article itself says water-driven mills needed a riverside and did not spread widely. It covers Japan only, not China, and says nothing of how many mills a town had or who worked them.

It states the waterside siting of the rice warehouses from standard reference works, which is why our granaries stand at the wharf. The kurayashiki was an institution of the commercial capital, where domains sold their rice; that a domain seat's own granaries stood at its wharf in the same way is this page's inference.

It says that cloth was woven at home but dyed by the dyer, that dyers gathered in dyers' streets in the towns and settled a few to a village in the country, that they worked at home to order, and that their indigo vats were sunk in the ground four together and warmed by fire pots - which is why a town keeps a dyer and why the dyer's vats fit his house. Signed modern reference entries on Japan alone, nothing on China, and on the early modern (Edo) dyer: the entries date the four sunk vats and their fire pots to the early modern period, and say dyers settled in villages only as cotton spread in the Edo period (before that, travelling dyers visited), while the medieval dyer grew his own indigo and did every step himself; the Nipponica adds that rural households making their own cloth sometimes did the whole dyeing themselves, their vats warmed only by the weather. They give no yard size.

It is used for the saying that a dyer's promised day could not be trusted because dyeing depended on the weather. The article says only that the weather delayed the work. It says nothing about drying cloth, so the step from this saying to a dyer's need for open drying ground is this project's inference. Two citations, neither attached to the passage on the saying, which is unsourced on the page.

It says the name most often marks the ward of an early-modern castle town where the dyers were settled together when the town was laid out by trade, and the list shows the name was widespread across Japan. Its account of the name carries no citation (its four footnotes are about single wards, three of them from a hobby blog), and the list is of place names, some of them former names. It says itself that the name also occurs outside castle towns, so it is no count of castle towns with a dyers' ward. It says nothing of any one ward's size or of water.

It says the timber trade arose where consumers and good water transport met, that the timber merchants' quarters were called kiba, and that the retail timber dealer kept sawyers and raftsmen and was found scattered everywhere - which is why a big timber yard stands on water. That a small retail yard need not is our inference: the entry has even the retail dealer keeping raftsmen to move his timber. A signed encyclopedia summary on Japan, whose one listed reference is a history of Edo's Kiba, so its timber quarter and its retail dealer with sawyers and raftsmen are the great Edo-period city's, not a small town's; it gives no yard size and says nothing of China.

It is used for the Horikawa, a channel about 12 m (4 jō) wide that served Kyoto's timber merchants as a log pond - a timber store on a city watercourse rather than a great river. Its limits: the Horikawa was not an ordinary stream but streams recut into a canal along a street of the planned grid of Heian-kyō, the imperial capital, when it was built in 794, so the width is that of a capital's engineered canal, not of a town's natural stream; the width is the Heian-era channel's (the article's 当時, "at that time"; it is mostly culverted now), while the log pond as the timber guild's monopoly is dated 1459; and the article hedges it ("it is said it could serve as a log pond") and footnotes it to a web page of a Kyoto tax accountants' cooperative relaying the Kyoto Saga Timber History (1972), a history published by a Kyoto timber firm - reported, not measured or excavated.

It says put-out weaving was a rural industry, done by farm households as a side job in the slack season, and that the clothier's own weaving was a household industry - which is why weaving draws as houses and not as a works. It says the arrangements are still a question for textile history; it gives no dates or numbers.

It is the example of a city quarter of weaving houses bound in a guild of high-loom (takabata) weavers, and in the Edo period it was the country's leading silk-weaving district. It was not the only one: by the page's own account Sakai and Hakata also wove silk, and after the 1730 fire Tango, Nagahama and Kiryu grew into rival weaving districts. It is good for the quarter's history and its guilds, and says nothing of the quarter's extent, street plan or houses. It describes the imperial capital's luxury trade, a ceiling rather than a provincial norm, and gives no house or loom counts. Its Meiji and later material (Jacquard looms from 1873, power looms from about 1887, synthetic dyes) is modern and does not apply to the setting.

It is used for the last step of the making, the wet sheets brushed one by one onto drying boards and set in the sun, which is the paper maker's visible yard. The Heibonsha entry names sun-drying on boards as the traditional method, against drying on heated iron plates brought in after Meiji. It is the Japanese practice: a town modeled on China takes it only as an analog, since the Ming treatise Tiangong Kaiwu (1637) records the wet sheets dried on a heated brick wall instead. It gives no board size or count.

It says where the tea stalls stood - the roadside, the temple and shrine precincts and gates, the crowded amusement quarters - and that most were stalls whose keepers lived elsewhere, some open only in blossom season, which is why a tea stall is placed by where the crowd is and may be drawn as a light stall. Their examples are all from Japan's great cities in the mid-to-late Edo period: Edo's Ryogoku, Asakusa and Ueno from about 1740-1770, and Kyoto's Gion and Shijo riverbed. They show where tea stalls stood in a metropolis, not how many a town or village had. They are Japanese only and say nothing about China's roadside tea stalls.

It gives both halves of the setting's frame: the Japanese drinking house of the later Edo period, found everywhere and in Osaka even on the bridges, and the Chinese wine shop, which spread with the towns and market towns of the Song and stood across the country under the Yuan, Ming and Qing, marked by a blue flag. The Osaka bridges are hedged as hearsay ("it is said") and describe a great city, not a small town. The entry states the blue flag in its paragraph on Tang Chang'an, as the common usage, and does not repeat it for the Song-to-Qing town and market-town shop. The entries give no counts for a small town.

It gives Edo more than 1,800 drinking houses in the 1820s and says the countryside was slow to get them, not until the later eighteenth century - the contrast between a great city and a village. Both claims rest on one popular book, Koizumi Takeo's 酒と日本人 (Chūō Kōron Shinsha), and the page gives the Edo count as hearsay ("is said to have been"), not from a named survey. The count is also for Edo, a city of about a million people and the largest of its day, so it is a different scale of place from our towns and cities and cannot be carried over one-to-one.

It names where Kyoto's restaurants stood - before the gate of the Gion shrine and along the Takase canal - an example of eating houses at a shrine gate and, many of them, along a canal. At the gate it names one pair of houses, the Niken-chaya ("two teahouses"), not a cluster; and it lists famous houses, drawing on Bakin's Kiryo manroku (1802), not a count or map of where eating houses stood. A signed encyclopedia entry on the great cities' fine restaurants of the late Edo period (after 1764), not a small town's eating house or an earlier era's.
It says those Edo eating houses stood in the cities and along the highways, which is where a map puts them. Its history is one sentence, citing two books not read here.

It is the one readable page found that counts a small castle town's smiths against its other trades from a dated register. Its limits are that it counts two streets rather than the town - the craftsmen's quarter, one street named for its smiths, so smiths are concentrated there by design - that it names only the leading trades (8 smiths, 5 physicians, 3 coopers, 2 horse doctors, "and so on") for 18 of the 50 houses, so it carries smiths as the most numerous trade on those streets and not a full or town-wide count of trades, and that its 2-ken frontage is the small end of a range, not every craftsman's house.
It states that Edo ashigaru stood below samurai status. The Edo-period section the quoted sentence sits in carries the encyclopedia's own insufficient-sources notice.

Three standard reference dictionaries agree on what the storehouse was and who ran it, and one quotes a period manual on where it stood. Their limits are that the siting passage is one manual's rule; that they give no size and no count of how many villages shared one; and that what they describe changed within the Edo period and says nothing of earlier times. The storehouse first held tax rice for a short time before it was shipped. It became a famine-reserve granary only after the Tenmei famine of the 1780s. Until the shogunate's 1789 order that villages build their own, the village officials' private storehouses were often used instead.

Standard reference dictionaries give both the Japanese and the Chinese institution on one page. Their limits are that the Aizu date is given as "it is said"; that they describe an institution, not the building or where it stood; and that the Sui start comes from one line of the Daijisen, while the encyclopedias on the same page say the Sui granary gave grain free and date the village-run lending granary to Zhu Xi's scheme of 1168, so a granary that lends grain is Southern Song or later.

It gives one seat of the Chinese village school, a building that already stands for another purpose: the lineage's ancestral hall, used for rites in spring and autumn and as the school the rest of the year. Its limits are that the ancestral-hall passage is not tied to a period or region, and its only citation is the transcript of a modern Buddhist lecture series (淨土大經解演義, archived 2013), a recollection rather than a historical study; and that the same article says most such schools were kept in the teacher's own home, so the hall is one seat among several, not the usual one. A closer scholarly source, linked from the article, is Liu Hsiang-kwang's study of Huizhou village teachers and elementary schooling, 1100-1800.

Four reference works, and a snippet of a fifth, agree on the watchman's duties and status and separate the village's from the town's. Their limits are that they say his status varied by place (commoners in Edo, mostly hinin elsewhere); and that they give no count of villages with one, no size of his hut, and no siting of a village's hut (only the town's, at a crossroads or beside the ward gate). They also give no amount for his pay, saying only that a watchman's stipend was paid; the side trade in sweets and sandals belongs to the Edo town watchman.
It quotes the Song administrative record on how many crematoria the capital had. The essay names no edition or archive for the edict it quotes, so the quotation cannot be checked against a text.

It is the smallest whole domain school read for this record - about 3,089 square meters - and its building list (a hall of letters, classrooms, a book store, sword, jujutsu, spear and archery halls, an office and a guardhouse) names no Confucian shrine, so it is the evidence that a school could go without one. It is one domain building late, on the ground of a converted official residence in the town. It is an encyclopedia article without inline citations. The missing shrine was unusual: the Nagano city history (長野市誌 第四巻, in its section on the founding of the school, 文武学校の設立) names it as what set this school apart from the Ueda, Takato and Takashima domain schools, which had one. So it shows a school could do without a shrine, not that many did. Matsushiro was a domain of 100,000 koku, so its ground is the smallest read here, not the smallest a domain school could be.

It says a domain had its great bell struck every toki (the page's own gloss is "about two hours"; the Edo hour was unequal and changed with the season, so it is not a fixed clock interval), day and night, that retainers and townspeople told the time by it and that it gave the alarm for fire, and that Matsushiro's first lord set it up in 1624 together with a fire lookout. The present tower is a rebuilding of 1801.

It gives the pair's first arrangement - the bell tower standing opposite the drum tower about 1,000 m from where it now stands - and says the bell tower served to tell the hours and that it and the drum tower to its west together preserve the Ming and Qing city's system of telling the hours; it does not say how the two divided that work. Its two references cover only the 1939 bombing and the 1996 heritage listing, so the 1384 founding, the first site opposite the drum tower and the 1,000 m distance rest on no cited authority; it serves for the arrangement, not the figure. It describes one city, a Ming provincial capital rather than the seat of the throne.

It sorts the Edo-period castles without a keep into four kinds - a keep lost and never rebuilt (Edo, Osaka, Kanazawa, Fukui, Saga), a keep base with no keep (Tsu, Akashi, Ako), no keep base and a three-story turret standing in for a keep (Yonezawa, Yamagata, Mito), and neither (Kagoshima, Hitoyoshi) - which makes the keep a form a castle may or may not have. It names examples, not how common each kind was; its only count is 65 keeps standing in 1854. Its section on castles without a keep cites no source. It describes Japan alone, where the keep appears from the 1570s, and says nothing of Chinese walled cities, so it bears on a castle modeled on Japan and not on one modeled on China.

It says where the trade of a post town went on - in its inns, under the name of inn servants - which is what decides that an inn town draws nothing more for it. Its 1772 caps are for four post towns only - Senju, Itabashi, Shinagawa and Naito-Shinjuku, the four gateway post towns at the edge of Edo and the largest in the country - and are no measure of an ordinary post town; it gives no population figures, only the statement (from a 1987 local history) that women much outnumbered men in two of the three Asama post towns, Karuizawa and Oiwake; and its footnotes are to 1980s popular and local histories.

It gives how many halls a Song precinct could hold and how large an audience one seated, and it dates the word's brothel sense to the Ming, which is why the Song precinct is not read as a pleasure quarter. Its sentence on the hall's box-like look rests on a quotation that compares a cart's box to a railing, and its count of thirteen halls in one precinct is from a Southern Song Hangzhou source; its "fifty-odd halls" is cited only to a modern popular guidebook, and in its primary, the Northern Song Dongjing meng hua lu, that count is across several neighboring precincts of Kaifeng, not one; its audience of "several thousand" has no citation on the page and in that same primary is said only of the largest named halls, not of a typical one; every figure is from an imperial capital, far larger than the towns we draw; it gives no hall's measures.

It is the one Edo-period public infirmary this record has read, and it says what it was - one longhouse of forty beds in the herb garden - which sets the Japanese form a relief house takes on a capital's map. It describes the shogun's own city, gives the building's type (a shingle-roofed longhouse) but not its measures, and says nothing of such houses in the domains. The forty is the capacity at the opening in 1722, given without a footnote; the article says the number of places was raised from time to time after 1723 without saying to what, so forty is the house at its founding, not the house of every later decade.

It gives the licensed theater count of the second great city of the Edo period: five licenses (芝居名代) granted in 1653. It also shows the theaters standing together on the south side of one street along the canal's south bank, with their teahouses across the street between them and the water. The five is a count of licenses in one district, not of the city's playhouses. The same district also held puppet theaters the article does not count (Takemoto-za from 1684, Toyotake-za from 1703), so five is a floor for a great city's playhouses, not a ceiling. The 1653 sentence carries no footnote of its own, the five theaters' names are later ones, and it gives no theater's measures.

It says what a Song entertainment precinct held - railed-off stages among shops, teahouses and wine shops - which is the Song form of a capital's entertainment district. Its references are three Song memoirs of the two capitals (Kaifeng and Lin'an), a historical dictionary and a modern popular guide to Song travel, but its footnotes attach only to the origin of the name and to its dating. What it says stood in a precinct is uncited here, so any detail we rely on should be checked against the memoirs themselves. It says nothing of provincial cities or of the precincts' size.

It measures the gate towers of a county seat - five bays, 14 m wide and 10 m deep - which is the smallest main gate tower read. The towers were all lost by 1948 and the present ones are reconstructions of 1997-2002, so the figures are those the article gives for the 1703 towers, drawn from a tourism office's page rather than a survey.

It measures both ends of a capital's range, the Yongding Gate's five-bay tower (24 by 10.5 m) and the three-bay tower of a lesser gate such as Zuo'an (16 by 9 m). It describes a capital, not a provincial seat, and several towers as rebuilt - Yongding's in 1766 and again in 2004 - so its figures are ceilings and a lower bound from one city. The article cites no source for these dimensions; Zuo'an's tower was pulled down in the 1930s, and the article does not say when or from what its measurements were taken. The numbers rest on the encyclopedia alone until a survey such as Sirén's The Walls and Gates of Peking (1924) confirms them.

It dates the clan temple to the Asuka period, which is what makes it older than the castle towns on this page. The article carries a no-reliable-sources notice, cites only a dictionary, stops at the medieval period and says nothing of clan temples in castle towns, which is the comparison this page draws.
